page.description: One-click UXSS issue with uBlock Origin on Firefox through element picker
page.text_excerpt: iter.ca • About • Uses • Accounts • Notes Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker By Smitty van Bodegom (loops) · Nov 15, 2026 Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details. GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC. The issue uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page. The element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html. That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters. Basically the attack here is: Figure out the element picker URL Create our own invisible (opacity 0) iframe that embeds it Drive the picker to put the filter we want in it Position the invisible iframe to trick the user into pressing the invisible “Create” button Figuring out the element picker URL On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation. Mosquitto is lightweight and is suitable for use on all devices from low power single board computers to full servers. The MQTT protocol provides a lightweight method of carrying out messaging using a publish/subscribe model. This makes it suitable for Internet of Things messaging such as with low power sensors or mobile devices such as phones, embedded computers or microcontrollers. The Mosquitto project also provides a C library for implementing MQTT clients, and the very popular mosquitto_pub and mosquitto_sub command line MQTT clients. page.text_excerpt: programming in the twenty-first century It's not about technology for its own sake. It's about being able to implement your ideas. Things That Turbo Pascal is Smaller Than Turbo Pascal 3 for MS-DOS was released in September 1986. Being version 3, there were lesser releases prior to it and flashier ones after, but 3 was a solid representation of the Turbo Pascal experience: a full Pascal compiler, including extensions that it made it practical for commercial use, tightly integrated with an editor. And the whole thing was lightning fast, orders of magnitude faster at building projects than Microsoft's compilers. The entire Turbo Pascal 3.02 executable--the compiler and IDE--was 39,731 bytes. How does that stack up in 2011 terms? Here are some things that Turbo Pascal is smaller than, as of October 30, 2011: The minified version of jquery 1.6 (90,518 bytes). The yahoo.com home page (219,583 bytes). The image of the white iPhone 4S at apple.com (190,157 bytes). zlib.h in the Mac OS X Lion SDK (80,504 bytes). The touch command under OS X Lion (44,016 bytes). Various vim quick reference cards as PDFs. (This one is 47,508 bytes.) The compiled code for the Erlang R14B02 parser (erl_parse.beam, 286,324 bytes). The Wikipedia page for C++ (214,251 bytes). page.text_excerpt: How Complex Systems Fail (Being a Short Treatise on the Nature of Failure; How Failure is Evaluated; How Failure is Attributed to Proximate Cause; and the Resulting New Understanding of Patient Safety) Richard I. Cook, MD Cognitive Technologies Labratory University of Chicago Complex systems are intrinsically hazardous systems. All of the interesting systems (e.g. transportation, healthcare, power generation) are inherently and unavoidably hazardous by the own nature. The frequency of hazard exposure can sometimes be changed but the processes involved in the system are themselves intrinsically and irreducibly hazardous. It is the presence of these hazards that drives the creation of defenses against hazard that characterize these systems. Complex systems are heavily and successfully defended against failure The high consequences of failure lead over time to the construction of multiple layers of defense against failure. These defenses include obvious technical components (e.g. backup systems, ‘safety’ features of equipment) and human components (e.g. training, knowledge) but also a variety of organizational, institutional, and regulatory defenses (e.g. policies and procedures, certification, work rules, team training). The effect of these measures is to provide a series of shields that normally divert operations away from accidents. Catastrophe requires multiple failures – single point failures are not enough. The array of defenses works. System operations are generally successful. Overt catastrophic failure occurs when small, apparently innocuous failures join to create opportunity for a systemic accident. Each of these small failures is necessary to cause catastrophe but only the combination is sufficient to permit failure. The 900-case follow-up ↓ Every conversation that could happen with a language model–every question, misunderstanding, explanation, and unfinished argument–produces a sequence of internal states. Could we map that landscape? Would conversations about similar things travel through neighboring regions? Would the same idea, expressed in different languages, arrive somewhere recognizably similar? Those questions led me to build an interactive atlas of Qwen3-1.7B’s internal representations. Before looking at the maps, it helps to know what is being mapped. The model breaks text into tokens – words, parts of words, or punctuation. Each token selects a row from an embedding table: a learned list of numbers that supplies its starting representation. I wanted to map thousands of conversations and see how they take shape in vector space. The vectors I’m interested in come from the residual stream, the model’s central shared workspace. The embedding table supplies its starting vectors, with one vector at each token position, and the layers read from and add to this workspace as they process the text. Taras Tsugrii’s chapter on the residual stream explains this perspective in more detail. In Qwen3-1.7B, each position’s vector contains 2,048 numbers.
